issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Verbal Access' conflicts with the other memory items. Being able to talk about the rape very easily is hard to reconcile with a profile centered on fragmented, unreal, image-based trauma memory and severe PTSD symptoms.

issues.item: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Story Feels Unreal' and 'Snapshot Memory' suggest poorly elaborated, emotionally overwhelming trauma memory, which clashes with 'Verbal Access'. This makes the Memory node internally inconsistent.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Physical Vulnerability' is less coherent with the rest of the profile because the dominant appraisals are global loss and mistrust, while the reported threat pattern is generalized anticipatory danger rather than fear specifically tied to bodily injury. For rape it is possible, but here it is the least well integrated appraisal relative to the other selected items.

vignette:
Valentina is a 47-year-old Salvadoran American woman who has been married for nineteen years and works as a social ministry worker at a Catholic community center in her city. She came to the intake session speaking quietly, her hands folded tightly in her lap, and described herself as someone who used to believe that helping others was the purpose that held her life together. That sense of purpose, she said, now feels like something she is only performing.

Approximately eight months ago, Valentina was raped by a man she had known professionally - a contractor who had been doing repair work at the community center. The assault occurred in the late afternoon, in a storage room at the back of the building, after the rest of the staff had left. What she remembers is not a continuous event but a series of frozen frames: the overhead light flickering, the sound of tools being set down on a metal shelf, the particular quality of silence that filled the room just before he moved toward her. That silence - thick, suspended, wrong - is the detail that has lodged most deeply in her nervous system. She has no fluid narrative of what happened. She told the clinician that she knows what occurred but cannot find the words to describe it, as though language itself has been revoked. When she tries to recall it, what surfaces are those still images, and with them, an immediate and overwhelming wave of guilt - a conviction that she should have left earlier, should have known, should have done something different.

Those guilt-saturated memories have fed directly into the beliefs that now organize her daily life. Valentina has come to feel that she deserves to suffer for what happened, a punishment logic she applies with quiet consistency. She restricts her eating carefully, finding in that control something that feels like the only domain in which she has agency. She avoids anything that would allow her body or mind to soften - rest, leisure, stillness - because relaxing feels to her not like safety but like exposure, like lowering a guard she cannot afford to lower. These strategies, in turn, have kept the memories from being processed in any narrative or integrated way; by never allowing herself to settle, she ensures that the frozen images remain exactly as they were, unexamined and uncontextualized, ready to resurface.

The memories also sustain a vigilance that has become exhausting. Valentina now experiences the silence of a room - any room, including the office where she meets with community members in need - as a signal that something dangerous is about to happen. When a colleague is late returning from lunch, or when a meeting runs past its scheduled time, she assumes something terrible is unfolding. She cannot relax even when she knows, intellectually, that she is safe. This chronic threat state has in turn reinforced her appraisals: she has concluded that the world is genuinely dangerous, that her perception of threat is accurate rather than distorted, and that she was foolish ever to have believed otherwise. The hypervigilance and the beliefs tighten around each other - the threat confirms the appraisals, and the appraisals confirm the threat - and her strategies of restriction and refusal to rest keep both elevated, preventing any disconfirmation from reaching her.

The appraisals themselves have become their own source of suffering. Valentina describes having lost her faith - in people, in the Church she served, in God - and says that the woman she was before, someone she remembers as genuinely happy, feels like a stranger. She carries a deep shame about what happened to her body, a shame she has not disclosed to her husband, who knows only that she has been "going through something." The distance this has created in their marriage is one of the concrete consequences she named: they no longer sleep easily beside each other, and she has declined every invitation to social gatherings their parish community organizes.

What finally brought Valentina to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago when she froze completely in the doorway of the storage room - now used by a different staff member - and could not move for several minutes. A colleague witnessed it. She is most afraid, she said, that she will never be able to do her work with full presence again. What she is hoping for, more quietly, is to find words for what happened.
